{{Short description|1859 mathematics paper by Bernhard Riemann}}
[[File:Ueber die Anzahl der Primzahlen unter einer gegebenen Grösse.pdf|thumb|right|The article]]

"'''{{sic|hide=y|Ueber}} die Anzahl der Primzahlen unter einer gegebenen {{sic|hide=y|Grösse}}'''" (usual [[English language|English]] translation: "'''On the Number of Primes Less Than a Given Magnitude'''") is a [[wikt:seminal#Adjective|seminal]] 9-page paper by [[Bernhard Riemann]] published in the November 1859 edition of the ''Monatsberichte der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin''.

== Overview ==
This paper studies the [[prime-counting function]] using [[mathematical analysis|analytic methods]]. Although it is the only paper Riemann ever published on [[number theory]], it contains ideas which influenced thousands of researchers during the late 19th century and up to the present day. The paper consists primarily of [[definitions]], [[heuristic]] [[arguments]], sketches of [[Mathematical proof|proof]]s, and the application of powerful analytic methods; all of these have become essential [[concept]]s and tools of [[Contemporary history|modern]] [[analytic number theory]].

Among the new definitions, ideas, and notation introduced:
* The use of the [[Greek alphabet|Greek letter]] [[zeta]] (''ζ'') for a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] previously mentioned by [[Euler]]
* The [[analytic continuation]] of this [[Riemann zeta function|zeta function ''ζ''(''s'')]] to all [[complex number|complex]] {{nowrap|''s'' ≠ 1}}
* The [[entire function]] [[Riemann xi function|''ξ'']](''s''), related to the zeta function through the [[gamma function]] (or the [[Gamma function#Pi function|Π function]], in Riemann's usage)
* The discrete function ''J''(''x'') defined for {{nowrap|''x'' ≥ 0}}, which is defined by {{nowrap|1=''J''(0) = 0}} and ''J''(''x'') jumps by 1/''n'' at each prime power ''p''<sup>''n''</sup>. (Riemann calls this function ''f''(''x'').)

Among the proofs and sketches of proofs:
* Proof of the [[Riemann zeta function#Mellin-type integrals|Hankel contour representation of the zeta function]]<ref>4 years before [[Hermann Hankel]] introduced this type of [[Hankel contour|contour]] himself for the [[Gamma function#Integral representations|Gamma function]]</ref>
* Two proofs of the [[functional equation (number theory)|functional equation]] of ''ζ''(''s'')
* Proof sketch of the product representation of ''ξ''(''s'')
* Proof sketch of the approximation of the number of roots of ''ξ''(''s'') whose imaginary parts lie between 0 and ''T''.

Among the conjectures made:
* The [[Riemann hypothesis]], that all (nontrivial) zeros of ''ζ''(''s'') have real part 1/2. Riemann states this in terms of the roots of the related ''ξ'' function, {{Blockquote|text=... es ist sehr wahrscheinlich, dass alle Wurzeln reell sind. Hiervon wäre allerdings ein strenger Beweis zu wünschen; ich habe indess die Aufsuchung desselben nach einigen flüchtigen vergeblichen Versuchen vorläufig bei Seite gelassen, da er für den nächsten Zweck meiner Untersuchung entbehrlich schien.}} That is, {{Blockquote|text=it is very probable that all roots are real. One would, however, wish for a strict proof of this; I have, though, after some fleeting futile attempts, provisionally put aside the search for such, as it appears unnecessary for the next objective of my investigation.}} (He was discussing a version of the zeta function, modified so that its roots are real rather than on the critical line.)

New methods and techniques used in number theory:
* Functional equations arising from [[automorphic form]]s
* [[Analytic continuation]] (although not in the spirit of Weierstrass)
* [[Methods of contour integration|Contour integration]]
* [[Fourier inversion]].

Riemann also discussed the relationship between ''ζ''(''s'') and the distribution of the prime numbers, using the function ''J''(''x'') essentially as a measure for [[Lebesgue-Stieltjes integration|Stieltjes integration]]. He then obtained the main result of the paper, a formula for ''J''(''x''), by comparing with ln(''ζ''(''s'')). Riemann then found a formula for the [[prime-counting function]] ''π''(''x'') (which he calls ''F''(''x'')). He notes that his equation explains the fact that ''π''(''x'') grows more slowly than the [[logarithmic integral]], as had been found by [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] and [[Carl Wolfgang Benjamin Goldschmidt]].

The paper contains some peculiarities for modern readers, such as the use of {{nowrap|[[Gamma function#Pi function|Π]](''s'' &minus; 1)}} instead of Γ(''s''), writing ''tt'' instead of ''t''<sup>2</sup>, and using the [[upper and lower bounds|bounds]] of ∞ to ∞ as to denote the [[Hankel contour]].
